=== FILE: Build Your Problem List [uQnigalG5dI].en.txt ===

well the internet has given us unparalleled access to incredible training unbelievable Minds the best technology it has also created a false sense that you can solve a complex movement or pain problem with three simple things you saw in a 30 second video on Tick Tock that is horseshit what I need you to do instead is start asking yourself what are the components to this thing build yourself a problem list then start Crossing that off the list one at a time so if you have a hot elbow is that because it's inflamed and congested deal with it do you have no rotation in your elbow at the wrist deal with it do you have no rotation at the shoulder deal with it is your forearm stiff deal with it do you need to rest do you need to clean up your diet do you need to clean up your sleep cross them off the list the bottom line is no one thing solves every problem and it's likely that as you start to address multiple issues in the problem-less system your problem will go away

=== FILE: Can’t go fully overhead？ Doesn’t mean you skip shoulder day. [Bs72rRX6VBo].en.txt ===

Working overhead is a human imperative. So the problem is while we all need to be able to work overhead, many of us don't have the ranges to be effective here. What we see in fact is some pretty clever movement strategies or compensations to be overhead without actually being overhead. Bent elbows, flexed or flared elbows, snake or banana back, for example. We all like the bottomup kettle bell press for stability and starting shapes, but it doesn't really allow people to get overhead. Even moving your hands apart on the bar still doesn't get you closer to working overhead in these missing ranges. My two favorite solutions are the landmine plus over pressure. Bring your head through your arm so your arm actually ends up overhead and the seessaw press which is sort of a variation of the bent press where we can press out to the side and then sneak into an overhead position. Both moves allow us to train without complete range of motion. we can kind of train with incomplete range but still give us the added benefit of sneaking into full or more complete positions. The mistake is even if you don't have complete overhead position, you should still be training overhead. That's the key. But we want to make sure that while you're still training overhead with these techniques and tactics with incomplete positioning, limiting compensation, you're still working to restore your range. So go to our app, take your overhead test, and start restoring that range of motion.

=== FILE: Don't Waste Your Air Squats As Unskilled Cardio [ZFOtUMg9Pco].en.txt ===

if you're going to take the time to do a bunch of air squats you might as well focus on some foot pressure and gain a skill that actually transfers look we love air squats they're great for warm-ups rehab no equipment situations conditioning but there tends to be a pretty big discrepancy in how people treat their body weight movements like air squats with how they sort of comport themselves in high skill High load complex movements we wouldn't just keep adding loads and Reps and speed to your front squat if your Technique was all over the place I mean go ahead put that on the internet instead let's add some skill back to your body weight conditioning in this case squats focus on maintaining your foot pressure evenly between the ball of your foot and your heel as you become more skilled there will be very little variation in your foot pressure no matter how fast or how many reps you do you're going to lose some concentration on rep or two that's supposed to happen the added benefit of focusing on foot pressure is that you can get thousands of reps that will actually transfer to more complex skills like Olympic lifting it also tends to clean up a lot of collapsed feet and knee wobbles too if your life depends on doing as many air squats as you can as fast as you can get it done by all means but if you aren't going for a world champion of the world slow it down until you start to develop better feel and better control then speed it up remember practice doesn't make perfect practice makes permanent

So SMART says the goal should be specific, measurable, actionable, relatable, and timely. So a SMART goal would say, I want to deadlift 405 pounds within the next six months. Okay. And for deadlifting 405 pounds from taking your deadlift for 365 to 405, that might be a great goal because like it's a pretty predictable path to get there for a lot of people. Maybe I won't. A better goal is to say I'm going to deadlift as much as possible. And here's the process I'm going to take to explore that. I know that there were some surprising findings from this study. What was the most surprising thing you learned in following these? >> The most the one that I thought was particularly interesting was that you know most people had thought that did the exercise prevent the slowing of metabolism. The answer was absolutely not. They still kind of during this sort of weight loss competition despite all the exercise their resting metabolic rate was slowing by a huge amount. But we were able to show that their total energy expendure, the total number of calories that they were burning was going up quite a bit because of all that exercise and physical activity. And then the thing that was most interesting about that phase of the competition was that people who experienced the greatest slowing of metabolism were the ones who lost the most weight. So you kind of traditional logic would go, well, if the number of calories that your body's burning at rest would goes down more, then that would make it more difficult for you to lose weight and therefore you should lose less weight. But in fact, the folks who lost the most weight experienced the greatest slowing of metabolism. In other words, the people who were most successful with their lifestyle intervention and able to kind of lose the most weight and keep it off were the ones who experienced the greatest response of metabolism. It wasn't determining the weight loss.

=== FILE: Hip Extension Test You Should Try Today [uEDYfe_2LMc].txt ===

 Hey, we're currently in a time where we are starting to understand and appreciate the dearth, the lack of hip extension, being programmed or thoughtfully sort of being assessed in our athletic population. Now we have a couple easy quick assessments we've talked about here before, laying on your stomach, bringing your heel to your butt, that's really looking at just kind of what's the sufficiency, what's the capacity of that thigh when I bring my heel to my butt. And my heel should go back to that thigh. I'm going to go very close to my butt without having to go very close to my butt without having to have the leg swing out or someone's back cranking over. That's just raw range of motion. But in that position we don't really have that much hip extension. That's one of the problems. But if already you start to flex someone's leg up and it becomes, you know, stuck at 90 degrees, you're going to have a hard time expressing that knee behind the butt, which is so important in basically any athletic endeavor and when we're tracing down low back pain and specifically knee pain. The second quick test we always have in this part of our assessments, formal assessments are sort of couch variations, couch stretch, putting my knee in the corner, being able to bring my leg up, being able to squeeze the butt. What we start to see there is all we're doing is same thing, bend the leg, but we're bending the leg and then seeing if someone can load the hip afterwards. And most of the time when people are doing couch stretch, they're not, it's a low level test. Like you should be able to couch upright, no problem. But most people are finding that they're still sort of, you know, working on the lower leg and that test doesn't actually look at how well the hip is going to extension. Hey, you're probably doing some form of isometrics. And if you've been following the Ready State, we love isometrics. We ISO everything, but there's an isometric you may be missing. Let me show you. You're probably comfortable doing a movement and pausing like a pause squat or pause isomemmetric hold. We love these long 30 secondond holds for strengthening tissues, making positions more robust, teaching shapes, right? They're great. But it's also important to do what we call an overcoming isometric, not just a yielding isometric. Yielding isometric means I go down and I stop and I can stand back up. An overcoming isometric is that I'm going to try to move something that DOESN'T MOVE. [screaming] AND WE LOVE those 30 second holds, but these are kind of four to six second holds. And what's great about this as part of a rehab plan or coming back from injury or trauma or even just, hey, I want to put some force in in the middle of a season without being kind of nuking myself is that it's automatically self-limiting. So when I have someone who's ready not just to work on positional tolerance isometrics, we can begin to load them meaningfully maximally at their available CNS tissue tolerance load with a simple overcoming isometric. === FILE: One of the most overlooked parts of recovery is staying connected to your team. 👀 [t-f5lcLh1cI].en.txt ===

This is a great example of highlevel psychology, high level sports rehab and real real emotional IQ. One of the things that we should be doing is viewing the brain as a survival mechanism that's really obsessed with safety, not safety, not performance. When an athlete is injured and we pull her out of her community, part of her team, suddenly that athlete is in the training room and no longer part of that daily training experience. That's essentially an existential threat threat to the brain. The brain is like, I have lost connection. I have lost touch with the people that I work with and fight with and train with. For a long time now, we've been advocating that if you have rehab, go to the gym. Go attend your class and do your rehab there. Do what you can do. === FILE: Paradigm shift away from Pathonogmonic cueing ｜ Feat. Kelly Starrett ｜ MobilityWOD [vUoKy0QNll4].en.txt ===

Hey, welcome back to Mobility Project. I want to talk about something that's been on my mind. Typically, we look at positions, problem positions, uh, breakdown mechanics. And how do how do we know how do we know there's a problem? I'll tell you. Come on over here. We typically rely on cues that we call pathonmonic cues. Pathonnemonic queuing means that I wait until I have a pathology that serves as a pneumonic that there's a problem. So for example, if you have a little bright little bite and you end up with a little bright ring around that bite, that's a a pathumic cue that you have Lyme disease. So physician sees that, they're like, "Ah, you have Lyme disease." Well, one of our pathonneic cues for strength and conditioning. Well, here's the problem is that typically the athlete works along and sports medicine's pretty much based on this. All of our kind of current concepts are based on let's wait. Oh, an athlete has a problem and let's see what let's see what's going on. So, how do we know we have a problem? Well, we typically see swelling in the joint. Oh, something's swollen. I must be doing something wrong. Or or the most obvious one, pain. Ah, my knee hurts. Gosh, is there something wrong with my squat? you get suddenly get squat itis. Further on, we see decreased range of motion, decreased force production, um, and my favorite, of course, which is numbness, tingling. So, you know, what ends up happening a lot of times is an athletes going going, "Oh, my fell asleep. Something's happened or I went overhead and and I got tingly. Is that a problem?" What we need to do is to develop an entirely different model of thinking about movement that doesn't rely on these cues because the problem is that the human being is set up for adaptation. If you've ever been in a fight, you can take some pretty hard hits without feeling any pain. Well, the same thing is true with exercise. Most athletes have suppressed a lot of that pain information, pain signaling. They don't get those cues that something's wrong until much later after the fact. I mean, say you're you're out like a young leopard and you're out hunting, you know, and you go and you bring back the mastadon thing and your friend's like, "Dude, you got scratched." You're not even like you're like, "I I got scratched. I don't even feel that." You know, I could scratch Diane Fu while she's weightlifting. She wouldn't feel anything until afterwards after she put the bar down. That's the point. So, if I'm relying on these positions or these these uh these symptoms tell me about my position, that's a real problem. Instead, we want to rely on understanding what is the good position. And this is why we spend so much time talking about getting the knee out into a better position. Making sure that the ankle isn't collapsed. Making sure that the athlete isn't overextended or in one of these open circuit faults or flexed in a bad position or the shoulder coming forward. What we need to do is shift our paradigm away from this pathmonic model and into understanding what it is we're seeing. Because if we're using pain, no pain as a as a cue that something's going on, we're going to be well into the disease or pathology process. This is why things like knee pain, uh torn achilles, if it's not pathological, if you know, you don't have, you know, a tick bite or a kidney infection or if it's not catastrophic where someone rolled into your knee and destroyed it, then chances are it's a preventable disease. And the key is you cannot rely on these cues to tell you're in a bad position. You have to know what's a good position. How do we know better positions? Because we test and retest. We get you out of those pathonic bad positions, the the using the kind of movement cues, knee in, we put you into a better position and you generate more force. So we let the thing that we're trying to change be the metric. And uh hopefully we don't see these things again. See you guys tomorrow.

=== FILE: The Biggest Loser Study： Why Exercise Didn’t Stop Metabolic Slowdown [2N2hI-Jv1js].txt ===

 and people have observed that especially in the phase of dynamic weight loss, while you're actually losing weight through a calorie deficit, the resting metabolic rate slows down more than expected based on just how much weight you'd lost. But at the same time, I was reading lots of popular articles and blogs and fitness magazines that said, if you just worked out enough, especially did resistance training and cross-training, you might be able to prevent that slowing of metabolism and therefore have greater success in weight loss. And then tuned into one of the episodes of this biggest loser TV show, which was this crazy television program where people are losing so much weight. And what you see on television is that these people are doing a ton of exercise, right, of all kinds, aerobic exercise, resistance exercise, cross-training, all sorts of things. And it occurred to me, if there was ever a case where we could study how metabolism was changing in the context of a severe calorie deficit with a whole bunch of exercise, this was the group of people to study. And so I eventually was able to kind of get a couple of postdocs in a collaboration with Eric Graveson's group at the Pennington Center in Louisiana. We sent out some postdocs to study season eight contestants of the biggest loser before they even knew that there were contestants on the program. But despite that resting metabolic rate still crashed greater than would be expected based on the reduction of body weight, which was a huge amount of body weight reduction. It was 60 kilograms on average over a seven month period. So 120 plus pounds of weight loss was the average weight loss that these people experience. And then the thing that was most interesting about that phase of the competition was that the people who experienced the greatest slowing of metabolism were the ones who lost the most weight. So the kind of traditional logic would go, well, if the number of calories that your body's burning at rest goes down more, then that would make it more difficult for you to lose weight and therefore you should lose less weight. But in fact, the folks who lost the most weight experienced the greatest slowing of metabolism. And that trend was also in place six years after the competition. The people who were most successful at keeping the weight off were the ones who concurrently at that six year time point were also experiencing the greatest slowing of metabolism still. And there was no relationship between the slowing of metabolism at the end of the weight loss period and who regained the most weight. So those were all very surprising findings because they kind of seem to flip the carton, the horse, so to speak, of what's happening with metabolism. Is it really determining who's losing the most weight or regaining the most weight or keeping the most weight off? And it seemed to be no, it was actually following that. In other words, the people who are most successful with their lifestyle intervention and able to kind of lose the most weight and keep it off were the ones who experienced the greatest response of metabolism. It wasn't determining the weight loss, it was a response to the weight loss. So yeah, so that was really surprising and something that was kind of totally unexpected. I always plan my programming about a week to 10 days out so I can be maximally flexible and adaptable. About 10 years ago when I was training for the Malikai, my coach started programming four big workouts a week. And what I ended up doing was recognizing that the days that they programmed for me didn't always work for the days I wanted to do the workouts or the time to do the workouts or or energy to do the workouts. So, I started moving the pieces around out of order to fit my desire, my time schedule, the energy, sort of how beat up I was. And what I ended up having was a higher degree of flexibility. That really worked well. So, man, on Mondays, I have a big big piece to do, but I didn't sleep well. I had to travel. I just move that big piece later on the week. What this does is this allows you to sort of think about all the work you want to get done during the week and then you can cherrypick as you go. You can actually have much higher quality training. === FILE: When Nutrition Science Clashed With RFK Jr.’s Food Narrative — Dr. Kevin Hall [s5fhrUPucnc].txt ===

 it was very difficult to get the attention of the folks at the leadership level of the Make America Healthy Again movement. And then we had some parallel research that was going on, again, looking at the brain mechanisms by which ultra-processed foods might drive excess calorie intake, in particular, looking at this neurotransmitter called dopamine, which is part of addictive processes. And the addictive drugs cause a very large increase in dopamine. And we happened to find that ultra-processed milkshakes, high in fat and sugar, didn't cause the same kind of dopamine response, which was part of this rhetoric that had been ongoing that ultra-processed foods are as addictive as crack cocaine or something like that, and we weren't finding that. And so shortly after the new administration came into office, and I'm still not having much luck getting the attention of the new folks to talk about our plans, we had this paper coming out, which was basically showing that ultra-processed foods might be addictive for some people, but on average, they're not giving the same sort of dopamine response in the brain as drugs, like cocaine or even cigarettes. And we kind of had some really odd pushback on that. I wasn't allowed to give talks at conferences and meetings on this topic, and I wasn't exactly sure what was going on with that. Maybe that was like a general thing, but then I saw some of my other colleagues were allowed to give talks and I wasn't. So it was kind of weird. And then we had this paper coming out, and we had a press release because we've been working on this study for like five years. And we had a press release ready to go, and that was like kill for no reason. And when a reporter actually wrote to us to interview me about this paper, she was denied an interview request. And the Health and Human Services Communications Director called the reporter and said, is this really a story about RFK Jr. because the results in this paper don't match his views on ultra-processed foods. And that was pretty chilling because it meant that the political leadership wasn't interested in allowing the public to hear about some of the science that was being generated at the NIH because it didn't mesh with their narrative about how ultra-processed foods work. And so I tried to get some clarity about what's really going on here. And eventually they allowed the interview, the written interview. So the reporter asked some questions. I wrote some responses in collaboration with my colleagues. And what was actually sent back to the reporter was edited and passed off as if I had written it. And it sort of downplayed the study and kind of changed some of the repris. It was like really bizarre. Crazy. Yeah, it was really nuts. And at that point, they were trying to get as many people to leave the federal employment as possible. And they'd set up an early retirement option, which I'd just qualified for. I'd been at the NIH, as you mentioned, for over 20 years. And they lowered the full retirement age to 50. I was 54 at the time. So I'm like, well, I'm going to write to RFK Jr. and the NIH director and several of the senior staff and say, look, here's what we're experiencing. This is the work that we're doing. We're sort of at the forefront of trying to understand diet-related chronic disease and why people overeat ultra-processed foods. We're making all this progress. Here's a proposal that I've been working on to kind of expand this kind of nutrition research for folks across the country. But here's what we've experienced, kind of the censorship and this misrepresentation of our findings to a reporter at the New York Times. And we're also now experiencing we can't even buy food for our research subjects because they cut the credit card limit of many of the purchasing staff at the NIH to $1. And so we had all of these kind of crazy things that were going on. And our scientific leadership was saying, yeah, things are going to get really rough. And in some aspects, they continue to be rough for my colleagues who remained at the NIH. And I said, look, if this is going to continue this way, I'm probably going to hate my job. I'm not going to be able to communicate our results anymore. I might as well take early retirement and keep health insurance for my family because otherwise, if I quit a year from now, I'm going to lose my health insurance. But I'd love to sit down and have a meeting and talk about these things. And I got no response. This was weeks. And so I started to wind down my lab. And I heard that people had circulated my email because a colleague of mine wrote and said, hey, are you really going to retire? I saw your email. I'm like, that's weird. I didn't send it to you. I said, no, no. It was circulated. People read it, but I guess they didn't decide they wanted to respond. So the date came for the last day to qualify for early retirement. And I basically submitted my paperwork and handed in my badge and basically quit. So the next day, the NIH director wanted to talk to me after there was some media kerfuffle about this. And I went in and chatted with him and told him what had happened and was raising the question of, we're in a state that was actually the same day that we heard there was going to be a 40% budget cut request from the president to the NIH budget. Because we see all this destruction going on in the scientific community and the biomedical research community. This proposal that we put together to improve nutrition science, if this really is something that you guys are interested in doing, would not be something worthwhile building. And he said, yeah, I'd like to work on this with you. And he shook my hand and he said, welcome back. And I said, I don't have anything to go back to. My lab is closed. But if you're really seriously interested in working on this, let's figure out a way that we could do it. And so for the next several weeks, I worked with the Office of Nutrition Research director and the Interim Rural Deputy Director to kind of put this together. And then out of the clear blue sky, that was killed for unknown reasons. So it seemed to me like this administration is very, they're disinterested in the actual science. And my view has become because science can only complicate a narrative. It only introduces uncertainty sometimes, right? And you kind of get, the knowledge progresses forward and you need this knowledge to kind of make the best changes to your policies or diet or something like that. But if it complicates the narrative, that can be politically problematic. And so my view from my experience as well as kind of viewing from afar what's happened with a walling off career scientist from talking with a briefing, the CDC, the former CDC director, for example, wasn't allowed to talk to career scientists because while the science can only complicate the issues. I just worry that despite all this political momentum and this public interest in improving nutrition and diet related chronic disease that we're not investing in the science and we're actually, the political aspects and leadership of this movement is actively disinterested in the science.
